title: Eliminate refresh for compiler-proven short-lived tensor pages
idea: Stop treating refresh as a service every page gets. The ML compiler/runtime proves that each activation or KV buffer is rewritten or freed within T_live (typically under 5 ms) and tags its pages with a page-table 'lifetime' bit. The controller's refresh engine then skips any row whose last write is younger than the measured worst-case retention minus a margin.
why: Refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 10-20% bandwidth, fact 3): 60-80% of AI DRAM traffic is short-lived, so refresh operations drop ~3-5x, and weaker-retention cells become acceptable for those pages.

title: Eliminate stored parity: decode weights against their known statistical prior
idea: Drop the 12.5% ECC parity for frozen model weights. The controller instead runs maximum-a-posteriori correction using the known per-tensor distribution of bf16/fp8 values (exponents cluster in a ~6-value window; signs and mantissas follow measured histograms), and repairs implausible words. A tiny CRC per 4 KB only confirms the fix.
why: Recovers ~12.5% capacity and tolerates raw BER ~1e-6 from cheaper, weaker cells on the weight tier; cost per usable bit falls ~10-15%.

title: Eliminate uniform cell strength: significance-graded capacitors within each row
idea: Fabricate rows with two capacitor diameters (a column-mask variant, not an extra layer). About 1/4 of columns get full-size pillars for sign, exponent and high-order bits; 3/4 get thinner, shorter pillars for mantissa LSBs. The data layout packs numeric formats so each bit's significance lands on a matching column.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): weak columns can use a ~40:1 AR etch, raising yield and density ~20-30% for AI tensors, where LSB flips cost <0.1% accuracy.

title: Eliminate retention binning on testers; characterize in the field instead
idea: Ship DRAM after only a short gross-defect test, skipping hours of ATE retention and burn-in screens. At every boot and in idle windows, an on-die BIST plus the controller maps weak rows, VRT cells and timing margins into a persistent profile stored in SPD/flash, and the system routes around them.
why: ATE time, burn-in and guard-bands are ~5-10% of DRAM cost; field profiling also recovers chips scrapped for marginal retention, adding several % sellable yield.

title: Eliminate the fixed wordline-low rail: deep-negative bias for hammered victims
idea: Give each local wordline driver a selectable off-rail (about -0.2 V normally, -0.6 V as a shield). The controller's activation tracker switches rows next to a heavily activated aggressor to the deeper negative bias until their next refresh. That raises the barrier against hammer-induced electron injection and passing-gate leakage.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): could raise the victim flip threshold several-fold without extra mitigation refreshes, recovering their bandwidth; costs one rail switch per local driver.

title: Eliminate ECC from the critical path: speculative data use with rollback
idea: Forward raw data to the core immediately and run a much stronger, slower code (2-symbol RS or LDPC over 256 B) in parallel. A detected error squashes dependent instructions, as a branch mispredict does, and replays them with corrected data.
why: Lets vendors ship cells with 10-100x higher raw BER (weaker capacitors, lower VARY) at zero average latency cost; ~10-20% cost per bit from relaxed cell specs.

title: Eliminate digitization: store neural weights as raw analog charge
idea: Write each inference-weight cell to one level on a continuum of charge (one DAC write, no bit slicing) and read it through an ADC straight into the MAC datapath. Decay and noise act as weight noise that the network is trained to tolerate (noise-injection training). The cells are periodically rewritten from a master copy instead of refreshed.
why: ~4-6 effective bits per cell with no ECC; 4-6x weight density on the inference tier, and errors become graceful accuracy loss rather than bit flips.

title: Eliminate scrap: sell out-of-spec dies as BER-certified AI memory
idea: Dies that fail retention or refresh specs are not discarded. Each is graded by measured raw BER and retention, then sold as a discounted 'AI-grade' module whose controller applies stronger ECC and shorter refresh. Inference clusters buy the cheaper GB.
why: Turns yield loss (often 5-15% on leading nodes) into sellable supply with no new wafers; a fast capacity lever during the shortage.

title: Eliminate in-DRAM parity: keep strong parity on flash, CRC in DRAM
idea: For read-mostly pages (weights, code, embeddings), DRAM stores only a 16-bit CRC per 512 B, and a strong Reed-Solomon parity block lives on CXL-attached flash or the SSD. A CRC miss triggers a parity fetch and reconstruction.
why: Frees most of the ~12.5% ECC overhead on the largest data class and tolerates weaker cells; ~10% more usable capacity at near-zero cost.

title: Eliminate spare rows and fuses: base-die CAM remaps failing blocks
idea: Remove redundant rows and columns and the laser/e-fuse blocks from the DRAM core. An HBM/CXL logic die holds a CAM plus a spare SRAM/DRAM pool that remaps any failing 64 B block at any point in life. The CAM is filled from test results and field ECC events.
why: Redundancy plus fuses take ~3-6% of the die, and repair is one-shot; lifelong, fine-grained remap recovers that area and saves dies with clustered defects.

title: Eliminate static storage: data circulates as a regenerated delay line
idea: Use leaky, capacitor-light cells (~1 ms retention) and keep moving data from row to row with in-array copy (RowClone-style). Each hop re-senses and re-amplifies like a repeater, so a row holds data for only one circulation slot. Reads are timed to the slot or served from the ring head.
why: Removes the retention-tail requirement entirely (fact 3) and lets Cs drop several-fold (fact 1); copy energy replaces refresh, and the density gain comes from the smaller capacitor.

title: Eliminate memory ECC for tensors: algorithm-based checksums ride along
idea: Append Huang-Abraham row and column checksum vectors to every weight and activation matrix stored in DRAM. The GEMM computes its output checksums as a byproduct, so a mismatch locates and corrects a corrupted element in place, and the DRAM itself carries no ECC.
why: Recovers ECC capacity and controller energy for >80% of AI memory traffic; ~1-3% checksum overhead vs 12.5% parity, allowing cheaper ECC-free dies.

title: Eliminate the hard sense decision: latch resolve time as confidence
idea: Measure how long each sense amplifier takes to resolve, using a per-column time-to-digital stamp; metastability time scales as log(1/dV). Slow-resolving bits are marked low-confidence and fed as soft information to a soft-decision LDPC/BCH decoder.
why: Soft decoding gains ~2 dB of margin, enough to run VARY ~20-30% lower (fact 10, ~40% less CV2 energy) or accept smaller Cs, with no extra reads.

title: Eliminate controller refresh timers: per-row canary cells trigger refresh
idea: Add one deliberately weakened canary cell to each row (smaller capacitor, leakier transistor) and write it to '1' at every restore. A low-power background sense polls the canaries, and only rows whose canary has decayed get refreshed, so refresh tracks actual temperature and leakage.
why: Most rows retain data for seconds; demand-driven refresh could cut refresh count ~5-10x and the bandwidth loss (fact 3) in proportion, with a self-calibrating guard-band.

title: Eliminate the end-of-life cliff: ECC rate that grows with age
idea: Partition memory into regions whose code rate the controller can reprogram, e.g. from 64/72 up to 64/80. When scrubbing reports rising error rates from aging, VRT or hammer damage, a region trades capacity for a stronger code and the OS shrinks its advertised size.
why: Allows shipping lower-margin dies and extends fleet module life 2-3x, cutting replacement demand during the shortage.

title: Eliminate module replacement: embedded microheaters anneal leaky cells in-situ
idea: Put thin resistive heater lines under each bank. In a maintenance window, the bank's data is migrated away and the bank is heated to ~250-300 C for seconds to anneal the interface traps and hot-carrier damage behind VRT and leakage tails, then the data is restored.
why: Self-heals the retention tail (fact 3), returning aged parts to near-fresh refresh needs; extends fleet life and permits longer refresh intervals.

title: Eliminate the storage-node junction: junctionless accumulation-mode access transistors
idea: Replace the n+/p junction at the storage node with a uniformly doped junctionless (accumulation-mode) channel. This removes the high-field depletion region where trap-assisted tunneling and GIDL create the leakage tail.
why: Attacks the <=13 fA tail (fact 3); if the tail tightens 10x, refresh intervals stretch ~10x, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: Eliminate weak-cell errors by storing safe states: data inversion masks
idea: True cells fail only from charged to discharged, and anti-cells only the reverse. The controller keeps a weak-cell map and, for each 64-bit word, picks one of 4 XOR masks so every known weak cell stores its non-decaying state. The 2-bit mask index replaces some ECC bits.
why: Eliminates most retention-tail failures without shortening refresh; could double the refresh interval at <3% overhead.

title: Eliminate unknown error locations: treat mapped weak cells as erasures
idea: Store the boot-profiled weak-cell positions for each codeword and pass them to the decoder as erasures. An RS code with 2r parity symbols corrects 2r erasures but only r unknown errors, so correction strength doubles at the same overhead.
why: Accepts 2x as many weak cells per codeword (retention tail, fact 3), or halves parity for ~6% more capacity.

title: Eliminate parallel wordline adjacency: rotate alternate 3D tiers 90 degrees
idea: In stacked 3D DRAM, run wordlines in X on odd tiers and in Y on even tiers, so vertically adjacent wordlines cross at points instead of running in parallel. Each in-tier wordline pair is separated by a shield line that doubles as the plate.
why: Hammer coupling scales with shared parallel length; crossing geometry could cut vertical aggressor coupling >10x, removing a key 3D row hammer threat (facts 2, 9).

title: Eliminate idle refresh: let data decay, repair at wake
idea: When a device enters deep idle, the controller encodes each page with a strong long-codeword BCH/LDPC and stops refresh for seconds to minutes. At wake it decodes every page, correcting the raw BER of ~1e-5 to 1e-4 that accumulated meanwhile.
why: Refresh is 16-33% of idle power (fact 3), and phones and laptops idle most of the time, so DRAM standby power drops ~50-80%.

title: Eliminate fixed one-cell-per-bit: dynamic twin-cell mode for weak rows
idea: A row found weak is paired with a sacrificed row in another subarray, and the two are written as complementary twins. The sense amp compares the two cells differentially with no VDD/2 reference, doubling signal. A mode bit sets the pairing, so only the weak ~1-3% of rows lose capacity.
why: Rescues dies that would fail retention or Cs specs (fact 1), adding several % yield and allowing ~30% lower Cs targets.

title: Eliminate discard-on-error policy: re-harvest retired fleet DIMMs die-by-die
idea: An e-waste and procurement rule requires that DIMMs hyperscalers retire at correctable-error thresholds be offered to a re-test line before shredding. The line re-characterizes each die, maps its faults and repackages the healthy dies (the majority) into remapped modules for tolerant workloads.
why: Turns part of the millions of DIMMs retired each year into new supply with no wafer starts; immediate shortage relief.

title: Eliminate DC bias drift: bipolar wordline pulses heal oxide-TFT traps
idea: BEOL oxide-semiconductor access transistors deposited at <=350 C suffer PBTI threshold drift that grows their leakage tail. During each refresh cycle, the off-state wordline briefly flips to the opposite polarity of the hold stress, emptying trapped charge every few ms so net DC stress never builds.
why: Removes the main reliability blocker for low-thermal-budget access devices and keeps their aA-level leakage stable for 10 years, so refresh can stay ~100x rarer than in silicon DRAM.

title: Eliminate domain switching: antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitor biased at transition edge
idea: Anneal ALD ZrO2 at <=400 C into its antiferroelectric phase, and DC-bias the plate just below the field-induced AFE-to-FE transition, where small-signal permittivity peaks (k~50-70). Read and write swings stay inside the linear region, so domains never fully switch.
why: Reaches the k~70 needed to break the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) at low AR; avoiding switching removes ferroelectric fatigue, wake-up and imprint; BEOL-compatible capacitor for stacked arrays.

title: Eliminate permanent breakdown: self-clearing nanometal electrodes on MIM capacitors
idea: Borrow the metallized-film power-capacitor trick: sputter a ~3-5 nm top electrode (Al or Zn alloy) at room temperature. The discharge at a dielectric breakdown spot then vaporizes or oxidizes the electrode around it, isolating the defect at a cost of <1% of the cell's area instead of killing the bit.
why: Lets capacitors run thinner high-k films at higher fields (more fF, fact 1) because TDDB events isolate themselves; extra margin for low-temperature films, which carry more defects.

title: Eliminate hydrogen: hydrogen-free deposition plus titanium getters for oxide channels
idea: Hydrogen is a shallow donor in oxide semiconductors and the main source of their off-current tail and drift. Deposit the channel, gate dielectric and passivation below 350 C using hydrogen-free PVD/ALD (O3 or plasma O2, non-hydride precursors), and embed Ti/TiN getter islands that trap any residual H.
why: Tightens the leakage tail and drift of BEOL access devices, raising worst-case retention ~10x and shrinking ECC and refresh margins; no high-temperature anneal needed.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: panel-fab memory sold by good-gigabyte
idea: Build oxide-TFT DRAM on Gen-8 glass panels with existing display tools, all at <=400 C. Tile it into ~1 cm2 tiles, each with its own tile router, and map dead tiles at test. Modules are sold by the panel's verified good capacity, and software only ever sees good tiles.
why: Panel fabs cost far less per m2 than a DRAM fab and need no EUV; tolerating 20-30% dead tiles makes their defect density viable, for perhaps 3-5x lower capital per bit at relaxed density (fact 4, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Eliminate litho-perfect decoders: stochastic address decoders calibrated after fab
idea: Pattern dense BEOL crossbar arrays with room-temperature nanoimprint, and build address decoders from randomly doped or randomly gated thin-film lines whose codes are unknown at fab. After fab, a discovery routine probes each line's response and stores a logical-to-physical code table.
why: Removes the overlay and litho precision the periphery demands (facts 4, 7) and turns random defects into table entries, enabling cheap, EUV-free sub-20 nm pitch arrays.

title: Eliminate per-tier perfection: vertical RAID parity tier in monolithic stacks
idea: In a monolithic stack of N memory tiers built at <=400 C, one tier in every 8 holds XOR parity for the vertical column of cells. A tier region lost to a deposition defect, crack or later failure is rebuilt from the other tiers on read, so stack yield no longer falls as Y^N.
why: Breaks the compound-yield barrier that makes 26+ tier stacks uneconomic (fact 2); 12.5% overhead buys tolerance of whole-tier defect regions.

title: Eliminate controller scrubbing: autonomous oxide-TFT scrub engines above each mat
idea: Build a tiny ECC scrub engine in BEOL oxide/CNT TFT logic (<=350 C) directly above each memory mat. During idle it walks its mat, corrects single-bit errors and rewrites them before they accumulate, with no channel traffic.
why: Local, mat-level scrubbing lets cells with 10x higher raw BER pass while keeping multi-bit error probability low, and removes scrub bandwidth and energy from the bus (fact 5).

title: Eliminate one-shot reads: NAND-style read-retry for nondestructive BEOL gain cells
idea: A low-temperature 2T/3T gain cell reads without destroying its charge. So when ECC fails, the controller re-reads at shifted reference levels from a per-region table learned from drift history until the codeword decodes, as NAND read-retry does.
why: Tolerates the wider threshold distributions of cheap <=400 C transistors at a tiny average latency penalty (retries are rare), relaxing device uniformity requirements several-fold.

title: Eliminate minority carriers: hole-free oxide channels make row hammer impossible
idea: Build arrays from wide-bandgap n-type oxides deposited at <=350 C, with no body contact and essentially no holes. The substrate charge-pumping and electron-migration mechanisms behind silicon row hammer then have no carrier population to act through. Qualify with hammer tests at 1M activations.
why: Could eliminate row hammer (fact 9) by physics, removing TRR and counter logic and their refresh bandwidth and simplifying the periphery (fact 7).

title: Eliminate wordline dielectric coupling: BEOL air-gaps between stacked wordlines
idea: Reuse the established Cu-interconnect air-gap process (a sacrificial polymer decomposed at ~350 C) to replace the dielectric between adjacent BEOL wordlines with air. That cuts line-to-line capacitance ~2-3x, and with it the coupled disturb pulse each activation imposes on neighbors.
why: Reduces capacitive row hammer and row press in tightly packed BEOL arrays (fact 9) and saves ~30% of wordline CV2 energy (fact 10).

title: Eliminate the fixed sense reference: pilot cells set each row's threshold
idea: Each row carries a few pilot cells written to known 0/1 values at every write. On read, the sense amp's reference comes from the pilots' current levels, the way wireless receivers use pilot symbols, so it tracks decay, temperature and drift of the <=400 C devices.
why: Removes drift and leakage guard-bands for low-thermal-budget transistors, extending effective retention ~2-4x and lowering read errors with no extra reads.

title: Eliminate final test: probe each memory tier before depositing the next
idea: In monolithic <=400 C stacking, add an in-line electrical test after each tier, using temporary probe pads on the top surface. Failing regions are logged into a defect map in the base logic die before the next tier buries them.
why: Catches defects while routing around them is still cheap, and turns per-tier yield learning from months into days, speeding the stacked-memory ramp (fact 2).

title: Eliminate EUV and single capacitors: self-assembled redundant capacitor fingers per bit
idea: Pattern capacitor holes at sub-20 nm pitch by directed self-assembly of a block copolymer annealed at ~250 C, and wire four cylinders in parallel per cell. A DSA defect that drops or merges one cylinder then only reduces Cs ~25% instead of killing the bit.
why: Makes DSA defectivity tolerable and removes EUV layers at the capacitor level (fact 4); cell yield follows per-quad rather than per-hole statistics.

title: Eliminate the front-end fab: US BEOL-only lines deposit memory on bought logic
idea: Buy finished mature-node CMOS logic wafers (including from U.S. foundries) and deposit memory tiers on them in retrofitted U.S. BEOL-only lines (MEMS, packaging or display fabs) that never exceed 400 C. On-die ECC and remap in the purchased logic absorb those lines' higher defect density.
why: Cuts new-capacity capital ~5x vs a DRAM fab and time-to-capacity to ~18 months, raising U.S. manufacturability from today's 1-2% share.

title: Eliminate per-company reliability qualification: national BEOL-memory test vehicle program
idea: Fund a shared public test chip and accelerated-aging method (drift, hydrogen, PBTI, disturb) for <=400 C memory devices, with open data and a JEDEC-track spec. Each startup then qualifies against a common model instead of spending 18-24 months on bespoke reliability work.
why: Qualification time and risk are the main barriers for new BEOL memory entrants; a shared vehicle could halve time-to-market and widen the supplier base.

title: Eliminate permanent vacancy damage: oxygen-reservoir layer re-oxidizes channel defects
idea: Place an over-oxidized cap (IrOx or oxygen-rich HfO2 deposited at <=300 C) next to the oxide channel. A periodic low-voltage 'heal' bias drives oxygen ions back into the vacancy sites that formed under stress, electrochemically restoring off-current and threshold.
why: Makes aging-induced growth of the leakage tail reversible, holding retention for life and allowing cheaper, less stable low-temperature films.

title: Eliminate parity bits: flip-bounded number encodings for weights in cheap tiers
idea: Store weights in high-BER <=400 C memory using a number format built so that any single bit flip moves the value only a small, bounded amount: Gray-coded exponents, redundant thermometer-coded top bits and a saturating decode. No parity is needed.
why: Removes the 12.5% ECC overhead and decoder energy for weight storage, tolerating raw BER ~1e-4 with <0.5% accuracy loss.

title: Eliminate interface traps: transferred 2D-semiconductor channels with van der Waals gates
idea: Grow MoS2/WSe2 monolayers on a sacrificial wafer, transfer them onto the memory tier at <=300 C, and gate them through hBN or another vdW dielectric with no dangling bonds. That removes the interface-trap population behind random telegraph noise and variable retention time.
why: Attacks VRT and the leakage tail (fact 3); atomically thin channels also give ultra-low off-current, potentially seconds-level retention in BEOL-stacked cells.

title: Eliminate single-device leakage tails: two series oxide TFTs per cell
idea: Stack a second access TFT vertically over the first (no extra area in BEOL) with an independently formed gate stack. A cell leaks only if both devices are tail outliers, so the tail probability is squared (1e-6 becomes 1e-12).
why: Turns the worst-cell retention problem (fact 3) from a statistical tail into a near-impossible coincidence, so refresh intervals can be set by median cells, 10-100x longer.

title: Eliminate separate ECC: lattice-coded multi-level charge across cell groups
idea: Write groups of 8 <=400 C oxide-TFT cells jointly as one point of a dense 8-D (E8) lattice of charge levels, as coded modulation does in modems. Decoding to the nearest lattice point corrects analog drift and noise directly, folding the error code into the multi-level storage.
why: ~2.5 bits per cell with a built-in ~3 dB coding gain, about 2x the density of SLC plus parity for BEOL cells with wide variation.

title: Eliminate TSVs and microbumps: memory tiers deposited directly on HBM base die
idea: Instead of thinning, TSV-drilling and bonding DRAM dies, deposit <=400 C memory tiers monolithically on the HBM logic base die and connect them with ordinary BEOL vias at ~1 um pitch. The stack has no bumps, underfill or die-to-die misalignment to fail.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss, fact 6) and bump fatigue under thermal cycling; via density is ~100x higher.

title: Eliminate fixed-function reliability: firmware-defined, fleet-learned refresh and ECC subscription
idea: Ship <=400 C BEOL memory modules whose refresh timing, reference levels, ECC codes and remap tables live in updatable controller firmware. The vendor learns drift models from fleet telemetry, pushes updates and sells this as a reliability subscription that raises usable capacity over time.
why: Lets vendors ship early, imperfectly characterized low-thermal-budget memories (as SSD makers do with NAND FTLs) while usable yield keeps improving; faster time-to-market for new memory.
